summary: spindle speed (Nₛ) is what the Spindle speed calculator works out, and it gets there from the diameter of part, the cutting speed, number of teeth and the feed per tooth. It is built for a materials order or a planning estimate you want to get roughly right first time. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Spindle speed calculator work?
sections.html:
The Spindle speed calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports spindle speed (Nₛ) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the diameter of part (D), the cutting speed (V), number of teeth (Z) and the feed per tooth (Fₜ).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Spindle speed calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Spindle speed (Nₛ)=1000 × cutting speed (V) ÷ (PI × diameter of part (D))
Feed rate (Fᵣ)=feed per tooth (Fₜ) × number of teeth (Z) × spindle speed (Nₛ)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Diameter of part (D) = 30 mm and Cutting speed (V) = 10 m/min. Working through the relationship above gives Spindle speed (Nₛ) = 2947.3138 rpm.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Spindle speed (Nₛ) = 2947.3138 rpm should be roughly the size you expected from Diameter of part (D) = 30 mm and Cutting speed (V) = 10 m/min.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in rotations per minute, and convertible to any of the 3 units on that chip.
  • Shown in meters per minute, and convertible to any of the 25 units on that chip.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Length, opening in millimeters
  • Speed, opening in meters per minute
  • Length, opening in millimeters
  • Rotational speed, opening in rotations per minute
  • Speed, opening in meters per minute

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Spindle speed calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Quoting a job where areas and quantities drive the price
  • Checking a supplier's figure against your own measurements
  • Ordering material and not wanting a second trip
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the diameter of part, the cutting speed and number of teeth — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Spindle speed calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns spindle speed (Nₛ), derived from the diameter of part, the cutting speed and number of teeth. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Spindle speed calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the diameter of part, the cutting speed, number of teeth and the feed per tooth, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter diameter of part (D) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Diameter of part (D) opens in millimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Spindle speed (Nₛ) = 2947.3138 rpm. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Spindle speed calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
